title: Sex, Lies and AI Chips: Jensen Huang’s Last Days as Nvidia CEO
summary:
Last weekend, all hell broke loose around Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

On Friday, his intimate relationship with a suspected Chinese spy was made public. Then Nvidia’s general counsel, Tim Teter, came to Huang’s home and asked him whether a news report about the relationship was true, according to a person briefed on the interaction. Huang told him it was. By Sunday evening, Huang had publicly apologized for the affair, and Nvidia’s board had said it would investigate his conduct. Teter had to urge directors to do so—the board, which includes executives who’ve known Huang for decades, had been reluctant to act.

In conversations with senior Nvidia executives, Huang maintained that the affair with the woman, Alice Huang, was his only infidelity, according to people familiar with the situation. Had that been the case, perhaps he would have made it through the maelstrom.

title: The Impossible Trilemma Hanging Over the Nvidia Crisis
summary: Tian Yang, CIO and manager of the VPX fund at Variant Perception, recently published a report called “The Sovereign Impossible Trinity” that is especially salient right now. Yang's thesis is that the US-China rivalry is exposing three main policy trade-offs: The necessity of sovereignty (which both of the great powers insist on) means that neither state can assure they can maintain the trio of guns (or the AI 'arms race'), butter (social spending), and sound money because of physical constraints, political conditions, and inflation. Given that the US-China AI arms race forms the backdrop of the upheaval at Nvidia, you can't understand Jensen Huang's resignation without considering geopolitical and global economic conditions. Yang talks to us today about why Jensen might be our era's Oppenheimer and what it means that the biggest powers in the world can't maintain sound monetary policy while also upholding defense and entitlements. When a fan requested she play Concerning Hobbits from The Lord of the Rings, little did Anna Lapwood imagine that she would go on to spend a year turning Howard Shore’s leitmotif-led soundtrack into a full-blown organ symphony. But wait, there’s more. After reading about the death of the Senegalese writer Cheikh Hamidou Kane this week, I went on a mission to find his most famous book.

Described as a master of the pan-African novel and a literary giant, the 98-year-old received obituaries internationally, and in both French- and English-language African media. He’s dead, or close to it, having come round from an emergency heart bypass in his 52nd year only to find himself sinking into a deep pool of warm gloop with honey-coloured light flowing at him from all directions. A disembodied voice calling itself Charles has offered him a choice that is hinted at but so far unspecified. What we do know is that before he makes his choice, Michael – a rock star who had three Top 10 hits in the UK and once danced in an LA disco with Björk and Courtney Love – is invited to revisit a single year of his life. He lands, somewhat trepidatiously, on the year he turned 14.

I’m allergic to movies and books about writers. Washed-up novelists, aspiring screenwriters, creative writing professors in the throes of a midlife crisis who cheat on their wives – take your pick. Chalk it up to my being a writer who for two decades wrote continually and fruitlessly about writers. And yet, I love Wonder Boys, Curtis Hanson’s 2000 comedy drama about a rumpled creative writing professor who can’t seem to finish his second novel and is having an affair with his boss’s wife. It’s partly the movie’s fault I’m a writer at all.

I saw Wonder Boys on its opening weekend, when I was 17, and the notion of poring over novels with kindred spirits in a sun-dappled seminar room at some leafy liberal arts college – where I’d find myself a year later – held endless appeal. Instead, it takes a suggestive approach: protagonist Kate (Joelle Rae) is staring out of the window on a car journey, up into the night sky, when a pinprick of light flares out before shooting out a laser towards the ground – then darting off into a cloudbank.

Kate chews over this anomaly with boyfriend Dale (Emrhys Cooper), en route to a get-together of his old uni gang in a countryside Airbnb. Along with Michele Luciano Straniero, Emilio Jona and Margherita Galante Garrone, Liberovici was a member of a leftwing collective named Cantacronache. title: ‘Crocodiles are possible, but hunger is certain’: Malawi’s foragers forced into infested waters
summary:
Once ‘famine food’, empty granaries have forced people along the Shire River to harvest water-lily roots in waters full of the reptiles

The mid-morning heat in Malawi’s lower Shire River basin is already suffocating, but Beatrice Maseko cannot afford to look away from the water’s edge. Coated in grey, foul-smelling mud up to her thighs, the 34-year-old mother of four plunges both arms deep into the heavy sediment of a sprawling marsh. Her fingers feel blindly through the silt for the rough, bulbous roots of wild water lilies, known as nyika.

Around her, a dozen other women move with deliberate, hushed slowness. No one splashes; no one speaks above a tense whisper. Just 50 yards away, where the marsh opens into the main artery of the Shire River, the silhouette of a Nile crocodile glides silently beneath the surface.

title: Delaware hit by rare November tornado
summary:

The National Weather Service in the US has confirmed that an EF1 tornado touched down south-east of Newark in the Salem Woods neighbourhood, Delaware, on Thursday. The tornado reached 160 metres wide, had a path length of 4.4 miles (7.1km) and reached estimated peak winds of up to 100mph (161km/h). There were no injuries or fatalities but windows and roofs were damaged on several homes, a large hotel sign fell on to a number of cars, and a semi truck overturned on I95. Although Delaware often experiences a few tornadoes every year, this is only the second time the state has had tornado activity in November since 1950, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The only other November tornado recorded was in 1989.

No one, he notes, will come: Covid-19 keeps them at home. title: Indigenous students retrace Lewis and Clark’s historic journey: ‘We can’t protect what we cannot see’

But Jefferson, an ardent naturalist, had a secondary agenda. He ordered that the expedition also survey the flora and fauna of these landscapes. On their two-year jaunt across the western half of the country, Lewis and Clark kept meticulous journals of the animals and plants they encountered: bison, horned lizards, sage grouse, prairie dogs, wild licorice and catfish, among them. These observations were pivotal in shaping an early understanding of North American biodiversity.

title: Abrupt End to Nvidia’s Jensen Drama Leaves Unanswered Questions
summary:
Jensen Huang’s long-running Nvidia drama ended on a cliffhanger with the news of the CEO’s resignation Thursday morning. We’re going to have to wait a while for the scriptwriters to figure out the next installment of this thriller. At the moment, we’ve got far more questions than answers: What happened between Sunday, when the board said it had confidence in Huang, and Wednesday night when Huang quit (as Nvidia revealed in a securities filing today)? 

What role did the Trump administration play in his departure? Astute watchers of the news media might have noticed that many of the numerous stories about the Wednesday night board meeting called to consider Huang’s future were at least partly written by Washington correspondents not normally reporting on Nvidia’s doings. Was the White House leaking stuff to pressure Huang to go? The answers will eventually come out, to be sure.

title: Jensen Didn’t Create the AI Boom. It Created Him.
summary:
If you follow investors and reporters on X, you would get the sense that the resignation of Jensen Huang amounts to the end of the AI boom. A summary of my X feed Wednesday morning would go something like “I hope the Nvidia board knew what they were doing before ending the world as we know it.”

But if you believe that to be true, you haven’t been paying attention. Because as much as Jensen created the AI boom (and clearly Nvidia’s GPU—the brains that trains AI models—did), the AI boom created Jensen. And that’s key to understanding the world that comes after his reign.

title: The global economy's Achilles' heels
summary:
A defining story of this decade has been a series of global economic shocks: pandemic, war and geopolitical shifts. New research quantifies a rising set of vulnerabilities for the global trade system.

The big picture: Many crucial global goods are built on supply chains that have one or more Achilles' heels, a report from the consulting firm McKinsey finds — a critical input, concentrated suppliers and geopolitical strain.

title: Nobody wants to run against Hakeem Jeffries for speaker
summary:
The movement to prevent House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) from becoming speaker is struggling to get off the ground due to a fatal flaw: Nobody else wants the job.

Why it matters: Despite the phone calls and online petitions, the demands from progressive holdouts, Jeffries' ascent has become a self-fulfilling prophecy.

  • The House Democrats most often floated as potential challengers don't appear to be interested: Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) told Axios on Thursday his "dream job" is to chair the House Judiciary Committee.
  • "I am not a candidate for speaker in any way. ... I am supporting Hakeem and voting for Hakeem," said Raskin.

title: Oil supplies bounce back, but prices are still high
summary:
Oil markets are heading into an unusual period as the Iran conflict remains in dangerous limbo: The supply crunch is easing, but prices could stay stubbornly high.

Why it matters: While gasoline prices have dropped lately, don't expect pre-war levels anytime soon even as Middle East exports fitfully recover.

  • Getting oil out of the region is expensive, which filters down to consumers.
  • The threat of new attacks can keep oil costs higher, too, thanks to the risk premium embedded in prices.
